speakerposition: topic
maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Prime Minister is in a position now to answer starred question No. 37.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I was not here yesterday. I promised to give an answer at the first opportunity and I had it available, but it was necessary for me to be absent. The questions are as follows:
1.	Are loans based on the principle applied to the Beechwood project to be available only for projects in the Atlantic provinces?
The answer is no.
2.	If not, will all provinces qualify?
The answer is that any province that has a project for which there is an equally good case could qualify in respect of that project.
3.	Are such loans available only for projects owned by provincial governments or provincial crown agencies or will they be available to private power companies sponsored by a provincial government?
The answer is no, they would not be available for private companies.
4.	Are such loans available only for new or uncompleted projects or will they be available for refunding obligations of established power projects in the Atlantic provinces?
The answer is they would not be available for refunding obligations.

maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. The Prime Minister said, in answer to the second part of the question, I believe, that other provinces would be eligible if they had an equally good case. Would he be good enough to enlarge on that and tell the house especially if the words "equally good case" have in them the factor of inability to supply the capital necessary for a given development?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the general policy, of course, arose in connection with the peculiar circumstances existing in the maritime provinces, where through the years there has been a realization on the part of Canadians as a whole that those areas did
not at all times equal the general development in other parts of Canada. Wherever there is a position similar to that, naturally the similar circumstances will assure that similar consideration will be given by the government to applications made by provinces.

maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Do I interpret the reply of the Prime Minister as meaning that, under the present financial circumstances of Ontario and Quebec, this policy would not apply to them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: FEDERAL LOANS FOR PROVINCIAL DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have given the general formula. My hon. friend will be able to determine the answer, on the basis of that formula, as to whether or not Ontario and Quebec would be in a similar category.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: ALBERTA

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ALBERTA
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. I sent him notice of this question two days ago in the hope that I would be able to ask the question yesterday, but because he was absent on important business I have left it until today.
In the light of the statement made only yesterday over the radio by Premier Manning of Alberta to the effect that oil production in Alberta is being cut back by 60 per cent of what the conservation board allows as a result of the present export restrictions on oil, would the Prime Minister make a full and complete statement as to the action the government proposes to take to correct this situation?
High! Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): I am sorry I did not have the opportunity of reading the statement made by


the premier of Alberta, but I am sure he did not say that any reduction in exports to the United States was the result of any policy of this government. I do not want to go into the discussions the premier and I had, but I will say this, that at no time did he suggest that the reduction in any way resulted from any action by this government.
As a matter of fact, what happened was this. There was a very considerable market in the western United States following the Suez crisis. The situation in California particularly, and also in the other Pacific states, was such that a very material demand was made for Canadian oil. Within the last few months, however, particularly within the last period of about six months, there has been a continuing reduction in the demand for Canadian oil in that part of the United States which constituted the major portion of the Alberta market.
The reason for the reduction is that there has been a very large increase in oil production in the Middle East and distribution of that oil in that part of the United States has had the result of reducing demand for Canadian oil. We discussed together what action might be taken, and the matter is receiving consideration and will receive further consideration next week when the premier of Alberta is here in Ottawa.
I think it was the day before yesterday that Premier Manning phoned me with regard to a committee meeting-an administrative meeting-in Washington that begins on Monday and will continue for two days to deal with this problem of oil imports into the United States. The convener of the committee is Mr. Carson. The Alberta government will be represented by Mr. McKinnon of the resources board in Alberta. The government of Canada will have an observer or observers at that meeting, with a view to ironing out the difficulties that have arisen in recent months in consequence of the Suez situation, and I am hopeful that action may be arrived at mutually agreeable to both.

maintopic: ALBERTA
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the representative of the government of Canada at this meeting to which he has just referred will have exactly the same status as or perhaps a superior status to the representative of a provincial government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any question of superiority of status on the part of any representatives. This is a United States committee, meeting as part of the administrative machinery of the United States and having for its purpose the design I mentioned. Any representatives there will be there purely in the capacity of

onlookers following the course of events and subsequently, of course, having the opportunity to discuss the matters in issue.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has his attention been drawn to an article in the issue of Time bearing the date of this coming


Monday, November 25, on radar defence of North America, which has appeared since certain questions were asked and answered in this house? Is he aware of the assertion in this publication that if there is an alert from the D.E.W. line in northern Canada there will be immediate consultation between the joint chiefs of staff in Washington and President Eisenhower, whose decision to give SAC's bombers at NORAD the go ahead could be made within five minutes?
In view of this statement being made after certain questions and answers in this house, can the Prime Minister not give us a clear statement about the position of the Canadian government and the Canadian Prime Minister in this event?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: While Time is most time-worthy, I do not get it ahead of time and I have not seen it. Regardless of what appears in that magazine or any other, the situation is exactly as outlined by the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: What is that?

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Would the Minister of National Defence outline the position?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house knows an integrated command has been established at Colorado Springs, with integrated headquarters, having operational control over the air force allocated for the defence of the North American continent. The air officer commanding the R.C.A.F. air defence command at St. Hubert has the actual command of Canadian forces. In the event of an alert, or of information being obtained by any source that hostile or unidentified aircraft are moving over Canada, the air officer commanding at St. Hubert has the authority to dispatch aircraft to investigate the situation.
While those aircraft would be investigating any unidentified planes, reports would be made at once to the government of Canada and to the integrated air defence command at Colorado Springs. Based upon those reports and the situation as it developed, action would then be taken according to plans which had been drawn up beforehand and agreed upon by the different governments according to the varying sets of circumstances that might arise.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. What about the United States air force, and United States planes in Canada? Would they be

Inquiries of the Ministry
under the same obligation to report to the government of Canada as the Canadian commander?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The squadrons of the United States air force now stationed in Canada are under the command of the Canadian officer responsible for air defence at St. Hubert.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: wish to ask a supplementary question. What would be the case with respect to United States planes based in the United States? Is it possible for them to be dispatched over Canada on the decision of the United States government without the Prime Minister or the government of Canada being consulted?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The consultations are already taking place and, as I indicated, a series of plans are now being drawn up which will be approved by the governments of Canada and the United States. If the situation were such that United States air. forces would be required for a particular operation over Canada, it may be assumed that that has been included in the preliminary plans and therefore it would be merely a question of advising the government of Canada that such and such a situation had arisen and such and such plans should now be put into force.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question arising out of the answer of the minister in connection with the Canadian command of United States squadrons in Canada. Does he mean by that that there is Canadian command over United States squadrons in Newfoundland, United States bases or leased bases in Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am referring to the squadrons which are allocated for the defence of North America now stationed in Canada. At some of those stations to which the hon. member has referred there may be other aircraft which are not assigned to the defence of the North American continent.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister whether the intergovernmental agreement to which he has just referred has embodied certain plans that are being worked out in regard to continental air defence, and whether that intergovernmental agreement will be discussed and agreed to in this house before it becomes effective as an intergovernmental agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that gives me an opportunity to review something of the past in this regard. On August 17, 1940, Mr. King and the president of the United States came to an agreement known as the Ogdensburg agreement. On the following day
a joint statement was issued. Mr. King referred to it and simply placed it before parliament on November 12, 1940.
Again in 1947, some 11 days after the house opened, Mr. King made a statement on defence co-operation with the United States and traced the history at length, but did not place the matter before parliament for decision. The only order in council made at any time that was tabled in the house with reference to this question was that covering the setting up of the joint defence board. In other words, in the experience of the past matters concerning security have been reported on generally. With the exception of the order in council setting up the defence board, which was tabled, nothing further was done than to report to parliament.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is not right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is the course that will be followed in this connection unless my hon. friends insist on a discussion of these matters. I leave it to their consciences to determine whether there should be a discussion on the whole question of defence and the arrangements between Canada and the United States. If the opposition will take the responsibility of saying they want these matters, which can be of dangerous import if given full publicity in the house, discussed in detail-

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No one has asked that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: -it will be done, but the responsibility will then be theirs.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: A straw man.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Would my hon. friends allow me to make my statement? In the past the course followed has been the one I have referred to. If my hon. friends want to depart from that course they have but to say so. We will then place all these matters before the house, and the responsibility will be theirs for what happens as a result of the widespread dissemination of this information. If either of my hon. friends, one of whom will no doubt be the leader of the opposition shortly, want the information personally or if the leaders of the other parties want it, it will be made available. I leave the responsibility with my friends of the opposition.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think on this side we have a full sense of responsibility in these matters and that we will discharge that sense of responsibility in the proper way. But in view of what the Prime Minister has said I should like to point out that the parallel he mentioned is not a parallel at all to the present situation and the proposed agreement.

Inquiries of the Ministry Perhaps the time will come when we will be able to debate that in some detail.
The arrangement to which he referred was a wartime one and it did not touch the control of Canadian forces in the sense of putting those Canadian forces under the control of an officer of another country, to which, Mr. Speaker, I am not objecting. I am just asking for information concerning the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Oh, no, not objecting.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister said that when we were in power we had not brought agreements of this kind to the House of Commons for discussion and approval, but I *would remind him that the North Atlantic treaty pact, to which he has already referred in connection with this particular proposed intergovernmental agreement, was brought into the house, discussed, debated and approved, and that it was in accordance with that approval that Canadian forces in Europe were put under NATO command under a United States general, or it might have been a British general.
This was only done after parliament had all the information which was available. No secret information was brought forward, because that would have been quite improper on security grounds. All I suggest is that we are now contemplating another intergovernmental agreement of that character, and that the house has a right to all available information which will not infringe on security.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend first referred to the conditions of wartime. I am not, for very obvious reasons, going to compare those conditions with the international situation today. But I do say this, and I ask my hon. friend to face the situation directly. Does he or does he not, speaking for the opposition, demand the production of the terms under which action will be determined? Does he demand particulars as to the degree to which the responsibilities of the officer in command and the second in command will be discharged? Does he want the production of the arrangements in that regard?
As far as the NATO agreement was concerned, as I recollect it the major reason for its presentation to parliament was that Canadian troops were to be taken outside Canada. It was determined in 1939 and earlier that Canadian troops should never be required to serve beyond the confines of Canada except with the consent and on the determination of parliament.
This is an altogether different matter. This is a continuation of the activities of the defence board which was set up. At no time throughout the years have its activities

been debated in the house. Indeed, it would have been presumptuous for us in the then opposition to ask for the terms. But I ask my hon. friend to be very clear and to answer this question. Does he, on behalf of the opposition, require the production of the terms existing as a result of the arrangements made between the governments of the United States and Canada on a matter that concerns the very safety of our country, information that I feel ought not to be given for very obvious reasons? Does he demand the production of that?

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question is a very simple one and easy to answer. The Prime Minister, the head of the government, bears the responsibility for deciding what will or will not be produced in the house. So far as we are concerned, we would certainly not expect him to produce any information in the house which would prejudice the security of the country or the alliance; but, Mf. Speaker, the Prime Minister surely is in a position to judge whether the answers already given to questions in the house on this matter have not been confusing and contradictory, and whether it is not time that the matter was cleared up.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a right to answer that.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker is on his feet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I say the answers have never been confusing or contradictory.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I notice the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar rising. As this statement concerns a matter of undoubted importance and the house apparently is interested in hearing a limited discussion, I suggest that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar be given the floor. Perhaps we could make the balance of the discussion as brief as possible, as I feel it has gone as far as it usefully can. Does the Prime Minister wish to say something?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I do not want to take advantage of the opportunity you have given me to answer except to say this-

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Order. I think the Prime Minister misunderstood me. I suggested that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar be allowed to speak first and the Prime Minister can make his. statement afterwards.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has suggested that if any members of the house, particularly the leaders of the

groups in the house, require information of this nature to be produced he would be prepared to do so. When he said that I thought he was certainly abdicating his responsibility as Prime Minister and head of the government, and that the government must decide what involves security or the welfare of our country. If we should ask a question which impinges on security, it is up to the Prime Minister and the government to decide whether an answer will be given.
I was going to say that I think the opposition

I mean the official opposition-is in a special position in the house. My recollection over the years is that from time to time when former prime ministers were in office, particularly the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King, and matters of this sort arose the official opposition at least was taken into the confidence of the government through the leader of that opposition. I may say that was further extended at the time. I am not asking for that, because we have not the status the Leader of the Opposition has. I think a great deal of this sort of difficulty regarding security and so on could be obviated if the Prime Minister followed the precedent set by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I think the point made by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) is a solid one, namely that if the government consider it unwise that this information should be given at this time, the responsibility for withholding it must rest with the government. They cannot ignore their responsibility by merely saying to the opposition, "If you demand that this information be given we will give it, and you must accept the responsibility." The responsibility) lies with the government. The Prime Minister, alone or with his other ministers, knows what this information is. He knows whether or not it will be detrimental to the country to disclose it. If he considers it unwise to disclose it, then he must take the responsibility for withholding it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: May I inform the house that if the Prime Minister speaks now he will close this debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, yesterday when we were discussing this item I was getting along very well until I just innocently, I guess, passed some remark about the trans-Canada pipe line and tried to put the responsibility where it belonged. Then there was quite a convulsion on the government side. In my remarks I did say that some of the press reporters were now becoming conscious of the injustice that was done on that occasion, and that at least some of them are trying to give publicity to the facts as they really existed on that occasion.
It is not my intention to go ahead and read the article, but I should like to point out that when I made reference to it yesterday I said it was either in the Financial Times or the Financial Post. I have the paper here in my hands, and it is the Financial Times dated Montreal, November 8. You will find the reference in an article written by "Tempus", an outstanding reporter, I may say incidentally, in this press gallery.
I was pointing out also, Mr. Chairman, that to a large extent responsibility for those unemployed in the construction work, the geological work and the survey work carried on by the department and by private industry in the development of gas rests with the policies of this government. I would hope
1414	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys that the Prime Minister, together with those who have responsibility for this loss of markets for the export of gas from Canada to the United States would do everything within their power to see that this situation is remedied and would give every encouragement to the export of gas into the United States so we should, in a measure at least, be able to solve some of our unemployment problems and certainly gain those much needed United States dollars which we owe to the United States.
I want to speak about oil for a minute or two. This morning I asked the Prime Minister a question with regard to the oil production situation. When he started to answer that question I thought probably he was of the opinion that I was blaming him and the government for the loss of those markets. I was not necessarily doing that at all. We have lost the market. What I was trying to find out-and I want to thank him for the extended remarks he made with regard to the matter-was what the government was doing or could do in order that we may be able to regain those necessary oil markets in the United States. I want to thank him again for the complete answer he gave.
When the hon. member for Calgary South was speaking on this subject the other day, he went to some length to point out the desirability of the government here and the government of the province of Alberta doing everything possible to see that the expansion of oil production in Alberta is continued, and particularly to see that arrangements are made whereby the exploration for oil shall be continued. He pointed out, and I agree with him entirely, that because of the lack of markets and the drop in our production, a serious unemployment problem in that industry is resulting; and of course that means an effect on many hundreds of people who are just ordinary small people and are certainly not those who are sometimes referred to as millionaires or multimillionaires.
There is one thing of which this house should be aware, Mr. Chairman, and that is that in the production of oil we are dealing with an industry that cannot, upon request, immediately start to produce the additional hundreds of barrels of oil that would be required in any case of emergency.
The only possible way in which we could meet an emergency-and we had an emergency during the last war which could have been disastrous-is through the continued exploration and continued development of our resources in Canada.	In
order to ensure immediate access to a supply of oil it requires not only months


but years of intensive study, exploration, work and development. Therefore this government should be very concerned with doing everything possible to see that the oil industry of Canada is permitted to carry on and expand its work.
I was interested in a remark made by the Prime Minister regarding a meeting which is to be held in the United States with a view to seeing what can be done to solve this problem of exports to the United States. In case, however, we cannot regain our lost market in the United States for the export of oil, then we should be giving very serious consideration to using our own market for the consumption of our product, thereby giving our own oil industry an opportunity of expanding both exploration and production. I am aware of some of the difficulties which might face us in this regard because in the eastern part of Canada, particularly in the Quebec section, they are importing oil which they can probably get a little cheaper from sources outside of this country. However, I do not think we should allow the safety of Canada, both from a military and an economic point of view, to be interfered with for the sake of a few paltry cents per barrel of oil.
This question is too big and too important to allow anything of this nature to interfere with the continued development of our oil industry. Furthermore, it seems to be the consensus of opinion today that the larger oil companies on this continent feel they would like to save the oil in Canada, particularly in Alberta, as a reserve for an emergency, and therefore are going to use all the oil they can get from other sources, especially when they can get it a little cheaper.
As I pointed out a moment ago, it seems to me that the large oil companies should take another look at this proposition, because unless we are allowed to continue our development and exploration, when they desire further production in this country it just will not be there. We have had to face a similar situation in another of our industries, namely the coal industry. This coal industry is one upon which you cannot call immediately for production to meet your demands. The industry must be kept in operation, kept active and alive, if it is to be in a position to supply requirements when urgently requested to do so.
I will not go into the question of coal at this time, because I understood the minister to say when the estimates were first opened that he would rather we dealt with this subject when we came to, I believe it was, item 238, under dominion coal board. I will

therefore respect his wishes in that regard. However, let me say again to the members of this house that this question of oil production and continued exploration would go a long way toward giving employment to those people who are now out of work because of our cut-back, and we should give this matter very sincere consideration. The government also should make every effort to see that our markets are regained for the export of oil.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the minister speaks I would like to say just a word or two about a matter in which I know he and his department are most interested and which has already been referred to in this discussion, namely the development of uranium mining in this country. This development, of course, has been spectacularly important and in its most spectacular aspects has perhaps recently been centred in the area of Blind river and Elliot lake in my own constituency. This area has now become the greatest uranium mining area in the world, and in Elliot lake there is growing up a fine, progressive and modern community which will mean a lot to that part of the north country.
I know the minister and his department will wish to help in every way they can with respect to this development, and perhaps one way in which they could help would be to expedite the building of a dock at Cutler, near Elliot lake, which would be especially important for the importation of coal for the mining area. Incidentally this dock was promised, without qualification, by the Prime Minister when he spoke in that area during the recent election campaign.
The Algoma area-and this is some indication of its importance to our economy-including Blind river and Elliot lake-will, it is expected, next year produce something over
14,000	tons of uranium oxide, which will mean a production of over 34,000 tons of ore per day from that one mining area. It is also expected that the value of Canadian uranium production next year will likely reach the figure of about $400 million, which will perhaps make it the metal of greatest value produced in our whole country.
The sales contracts covering this enormous production are practically all made with the United States government and as my hon. friend knows, are underwritten by the federal government. As an indication of the magnitude of this operation, I understand for that purpose sales arrangements have been underwritten up to the end of 1962 amounting to more than $1,600 million worth of products.
There has recently been expressed some uncertainty-indeed, this uncertainty was
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys expressed in this house last night-about the prospects of this mining industry. It has been suggested, and this suggestion has reached the press, that uranium as a source of atomic energy will soon be outmoded by what is called the fusion process, which is the joining together of two nuclei, replacing the fission process which is the splitting of the atom, and which of course requires uranium. It is also feared by some that the needs for uranium will be diminished by the development of what is known as the fast breeder process. Yet those who are informed on this matter and scientifically qualified to discuss it in a way which, of course, I am not, have stated-and I am referring now to the vice-president of research and development for Atomic Energy of Canada, Dr. Lewis,-that Canada's uranium future would not be in jeopardy through fusion, and Dr. Lewis went on to say that people are becoming confused between a scientific experiment and something which affects the economic future of the world.
Another fear has been expressed-and it was mentioned last night also during the discussion-as to what will happen to this industry when the current contracts, the magnitude of which I have mentioned, come to an end in 1962, a date very much in the minds of those people in this country who are working to develop these communities and this industry. I do not think we need to be pessimistic on this point. While it would be unwise to be pessimistic or to indulge in what I might call speculative optimism, yet I feel certain that the producers of this product in Canada will have continued markets beyond 1962; and perhaps it is a matter for some satisfaction and, in a sense, a reply to some of the more pessimistic forecasts, that the United States atomic energy commission which is, of course, a very important agency in the development of this mining has already secured options on Canadian production for several years beyond 1962.
I know, of course, as do other hon. members that the great bulk of this product is now going into military use, and perhaps I was in a somewhat incongruous position when I was Secretary of State for External Affairs inasmuch as in that capacity it was my duty and desire, as the representative of the government at international meetings, to do everything I could-and I am sure I had the support of the house in this-to make the use of uranium for destructive purposes unnecessary and impossible, but that at the same time, as the hon. member

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys for Algoma East, I was doing everything I could to encourage and develop the use of that product.
As I say, most of this material-almost all of it, in fact-goes into military use, and it is a matter of great importance that the government should do everything it can, and I am sure it will, to push the search for markets for this product for civilian purposes. To that end, as the minister knows, contracts have been signed with the United Kingdom and, I think, with the government of the Federal Republic of West Germany.
With the development of this peacetime, civilian use of uranium it will become increasingly important that the government should explore every possibility of reaching agreement with any friendly country for the use of this material, though, of course, every agreement of this kind, because of the nature of this material, will have to be reconciled with security requirements, and will also have to be in accordance with the provisions of the United Nations regarding the peaceful uses of atomic energy.
There is also, of course, the important progress made in recent years in the use of uranium as a source of electrical energy. That progress has gone farthest in the United Kingdom where, indeed, electrical energy derived from uranium is now competitive with the same power derived from coal. But the United States and other countries are also moving ahead in this field and I think we can feel, without going overboard with extravagant optimism, that as the use of this material for warlike purposes diminishes-and we all hope it will diminish-its use for peaceful purposes will increase, taking up the supplies of this product which are now going into the manufacture of weapons.
It is also a source of some satisfaction from a Canadian point of view to learn that we have the largest reserves of uranium of any country in the world, as far as we know at present, and it has been said that the United States reserves will be exhausted in about 10 years. I think it is not extravagant or unrealistic to look forward to the day when this uranium will be needed in our own country, to, as a source of electrical energy.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I wanted to put these facts on record in connection with a subject which is of increasing importance to Canada and the world; a matter which is of vital importance with regard to collective defence and which, I hope, will become equally important in developing means of collective progress, and I ask the minister to give every consideration, as I know he will, to whatever steps the federal government can take in this important development, especially, if I may

say so, with regard to that area of northern Ontario which has become the uranium centre of the world.

Whenever I order maps from the department, as I often do, I find that they are practically all printed in English only. I have no objection to that as long as maps are also printed in French, making them bilingual publications.
I have often examined the famous map showing the whole of Canada and I genuinely deplore the fact that this official map, which is certainly distributed all over the world, is printed in English only. In order to emphasize the truly bilingual character of Canada, the department should make this map bilingual, from now on, so as to give justice to both the main racial groups which make up our country.
I also notice that a map representing a section of my constituency, particularly the Roberval area, is almost entirely labelled in English, in spite of the fact that this particular district happens to be one of the most exclusively French-speaking in the country.
I am not making any charges against anyone but merely pointing out this fact in passing. Since the minister, his parliamentary assistant and his deputy-who are all in the house at this time-are all three Frenchspeaking, I hardly feel it necessary to labour that very important point. I thank them for the efforts they will no doubt make to satisfy us on that score.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks I am going to make and the questions I intend to ask relate almost entirely to the publications of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I should perhaps explain that my contact with the publications has been as a librarian, providing prospectors and geologists with the various publications, and the point I want to make arises from my experience with the publications of the department.
The first general comment I would offer is that the publications of geological surveys, especially the earlier ones, contain some of the best accounts of history that are available. Unfortunately they are buried in those publications, and I would suggest that at some time someone in the department consider going back into the early reports, especially those of the 1850's, 1860's and 1870's, to take from them some of the excellent historical pieces on the trips of the surveyors across Canada.
The first question I would like to ask is how much co-operation with provincial geological surveyors is entered into in order to ensure that there is no repetition and that the publications or the coverage of each supplements the other. I have the feeling that there has been a certain amount of overlapping in the past. Second, does the department plan a cumulative volume of the provincial gazeteers that they are publishing at the present time one by one?
My third question is this. Does the printer of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys publications keep the typeset for the major publication such as memoirs? I am very appreciative of the fact that some of the more important memoirs are being reprinted, but if the typeset is kept I think more copies should be reprinted, because especially early in the series they are missing and at least in our area where prospecting is a major interest there has been quite a demand for them.
As a fourth question I would ask if the print is not kept set for reprints, when a reprint is made is there any plan for revisions in bibliography and any later information in connection with the area in order to insert it into the text?
The fifth question I would like to ask is the following. Is the ore dressing section carrying out any research now on the treatment of low-grade iron ores with natural gas being used as the heating process? I know they have been carrying out quite a number of experiments with low-grade iron ores, but it is this question of the natural gas which has arisen in our region where we have many low-grade iron ore deposits. If
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys a group, say the holders of iron deposits, brought samples to the department for bene-ficiating trials, how would the costs of these experiments be borne?

Mr. Chairman, this appropriation provides for the administration of the Explosives Act and regulations thereunder. The act regulates the manufacture, testing, storage, sale and importation of explosives. By regulation the transportation of explosives by road and private railway is also controlled. The act does not apply to explosives under the control of the Minister of National Defence nor to transportation by vessel, aircraft or public railway.
The primary objective is to ensure the safety of the public and of those handling explosives. All explosives manufactured in or imported into Canada must be first authorized by the minister. Samples must therefore be submitted before manufacture or importation for testing and examination in the explosives laboratory maintained by this division. Explosives already authorized are regularly examined to ensure conformity with the formula declared at the time of authorization.

217.	Geodetic survey of Canada-administration, operation and maintenance, $577,258.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
There are two items or sections which might give the answer to that question. Firstly there is the economic part which is to provide for horizontal and vertical control by means of precise triangulation, precise traverse, shoran trilateration and precise levelling for the mapping and charting of Canada, so that all other surveys may be co-ordinated on a single datum on a nation-wide scale; to provide the horizontal and vertical co-ordinates and mathematical data required for development projects such as the St. Lawrence seaway, hydro-electric power developments, engineering projects, harbour improvement schemes, and oil exploration operations; to determine the position of survey stations in terms of precise astronomical latitudes and longitudes for control in the demarcation of provincial boundaries, for example, the 60th parallel of latitude.
The second is the scientific part which is to undertake investigations leading to a more precise determination of the size and the shape of the earth; to develop and test improved survey methods and improved methods of carrying out survey computations. To co-operate with other national geodetic organizations, through the international association of geodesy, in the solution of problems in geodesy such as the mathematical solution of long geodetic lines, the adjustment of shoran nets of trilateration, and the determination of the attainable precision in various types of geodetic work.

On this vote, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief reference to the grounding of C.G.S. Baffin on Black rock, a well marked obstruction off the coast of Nova Scotia on July 4, last. In so far as the hydrographic survey is concerned, I have in the last eight years had many contacts with the officials of the department and I have always found them very efficient and courteous, and I should judge from the report given by the minister on November 11 last, that the minister's finding is the same. I do know that the work being done is greatly appreciated along our coast.
But there is one matter we cannot understand, and that is how a ship equipped with all the modern electronic and navigational aids such as the Baffin has could run into such a difficulty. The report the minister gave on November 11 has one sentence in it that I should like to bring to the attention of the house. An inquiry was held, and the report brought out the fact that the grounding was due to a combination of circumstances but not to any negligence on the part of the hydrographic officers navigating the ship. From my knowledge of those navigating officers and of the hydrographic staff I do not find that hard to understand, but from the point of view of those who write articles and editorials in newspapers in the province of Nova Scotia, it is more difficult to follow.
What was this peculiar combination of circumstances which caused the grounding of the ship? Two or three days ago I asked the Minister of Transport if he would be willing to table the report of the inquiry which was carried out by his department-the report to which the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys referred to on November 11- but the Minister of Transport said the report was not a report made under the Canada Shipping Act; that it had been carried out by one of the officers of his department and, as such, he did not consider it appropriate for publication. But I think there are a great many Nova Scotians along the coast who are very much interested in the cause or causes of this grounding. The ship had all the modern navigational aids, and, as the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys said in his statement, they were the type of aids used on another ship, the Kapuskasing, and they had been found very accurate.
It may well be that something unusual occurred in the use of these instruments. They may have been found defective, and if so I think we are entitled to know, because instruments of this type are being used by


fishing boats and many other types of ships all along our coast. If anything of this nature caused the trouble I think it would be for the good of the public to know whether fives are being endangered or public property being subjected to undue risk. That being so, may I ask the minister if he will table a report and give us a full explanation of what he means by the phrase "a combination of circumstances".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I will certainly table the report. I cannot say it will be the report of the Department of Transport but it will be the report we have in our department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

Anyone can cut his finger on a very good knife. It was just a mistake or a misinterpretation. I think the public would like to know just where the dividing line runs in the duties, responsibilities and authority of these two individuals. For example, which one of them is regarded as the senior officer? Which one is regarded as being responsible for the safety of the ship and the safety and fives of the crew? Who decides when the boat shall sail, when it shall anchor and

where it shall anchor? Who decides when it is fit to lower the boats and land men on a lee shore? There is some feeling that part of the confusion to which the minister has referred is attributable to the confusion in command and I think it would be well for the minister to clear that up.

I did not quite understand what his answer was in that respect but the question I want him to clarify is this. Just what was happening to the instruments? Did they fail? Were they not accurate? Was the captain in charge of the ship relying solely on instruments and was he not taking the usual precautions which every navigator would take regardless of instruments?

Mr. Chairman, I have a matter which I consider to be very important to bring to the attention of the minister. As he may or may not be aware the boundary between Newfoundland-Labrador and Quebec has never been settled. Newfoundland was awarded a large part of the Labrador territory by a decision of the privy council many years ago. There was not a dispute but a disagreement as to who had jurisdiction over large sections of Labrador, and many years ago a case was taken to the privy council for decision. That course was agreed to by the province of Quebec and by the dominion, as it then was, of Newfoundland.
As a consequence of that decision, which was incorporated in the terms of union, the boundary between the province of Quebec and Newfoundland-Labrador has never been properly defined. I have no desire to raise any quarrel between Quebec and Newfoundland but, as the minister is probably aware, big mineral developments are taking place in this territory. I understand that there are huge iron ore deposits on both sides of the border so that these companies eventually, and probably pretty soon, will have to find out to whom they are to pay their royalties, whether to the province of Newfoundland or the province of Quebec.
I know that this may not be the minister's responsibility but I was given to understand that such surveys are made by the minister's department on request from the provinces. This matter has not reached the stage yet where it is very important but it will soon. Speaking as far as Newfoundland is concerned, may I say that we do not want one inch of territory from Quebec to which we are not entitled. The minister's department may be called upon to carry out such a survey. It is a question that could properly be asked of every one of the ministers whose estimates we are asked to consider. Common sense tells us that our main function at this time is to approve only those estimates which are absolutely essential to the maintenance of indispensable services. I think the only protection that the taxpayer of this country has is that we make careful examination of the mass of figures that are submitted to us in these estimates.
In order to protect the taxpayer's purse I think we ought to have a little bit of information with respect to the computation of these figures. I think one of the dangers in the manner of examining these estimates is that they are brought into the house and after a few political speeches on the need for spending more money on some pet local projects, they are passed. I think we would be fooling ourselves if we were to adopt the attitude that there is no waste in federal bureaucracy. This is no reflection on the dedicated men and women who are in the civil service, but it is a reflection on the situation which is a natural consequence of extravagant and ever-growing government in the past 22 years. Therefore in this connection I should like to ask the minister in what manner are some of these cost items determined in connection with item 227? What manner of checking is used to determine these to be indispensable? Are these estimates of costs submitted on the basis of current prices and wages or do they contain probable increases; if so, what percentage-wise?

I am not opposed to essential spending, but it seems to me that we are considering the original estimates of the previous Liberal government and the question is, is this a government which is dedicated to eliminating waste and extravagance? speechtext:
May I first congratulate personally the minister for having been called as a member of the present cabinet. Then may I refer to a recent book entitled "Prospecting in Canada" published by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. My request would be for a translation of said work and for its distribution in our high schools and our libraries so that this very up to date publication may be available also in the French language for distribution at the earliest possible time. Many people in the district of Abitibi which I represent here will thus obtain considerable information which would eventually allow them to take a more effective part in connection with research and the development of new mineral deposits, be it for iron, zinc, gold or copper.
The minister is also requested to offer the public more publications in both the English language and the French language. This would be useful for more than one area in the province of Quebec at least. The publication to which I referred, namely "Prospecting in Canada" by A. H. Lang, published in 1956, publication No. 2529, contributes to the expansion of the Canadian mineral industry and to the success of many prospectors, students and companies. It includes very interesting data on the stature of Canada's mineral industry. It refers to prospectors of the past, prospectors of today and prospectors of the future. Conventional methods of prospecting and special methods also are explained in the publication. More particularly I refer to geophysical prospecting methods, the dip needle, the gravity method, seismic methods and electrical induction methods. It compares ground and airborne magnetometer surveys.
In view of the very interesting discovery in Chapleau riding of zinc and iron ore deposits lately, we ask the minister if he will order a helicopter-equipped party to complete more topographical mapping along the Harricana river and also along the Not-taway river which both flow towards James bay. Such mapping in the area north of lake Mattagami would permit more complete and adequate knowledge about possible hydraulic development associated with other mining and industrial projects of interest at the present time for the Harricana and lake Mattagami areas.
This would undoubtedly be useful at this time for the provincial authorities who, we are told, are considering the possibility of authorizing industrial development in the area.

He gave a very optimistic report about the development of the tar sands. He had spent some 20 years up there, and was a master of the subject. As I say, he spoke in glowing terms, and the committee was completely prepared to make a recommendation regarding the development of these sands, but the next day another official, another officer from the department, a man who was apparently Doctor Ells superior, poured cold water over the whole thing and suggested we

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys should forget all about it. Dr. Ells had suggested the steam pressure method of extracting the oil but, as I say, the next day another official came, a man who was apparently the superior of Dr. Ells and poured cold water over the whole thing.

speechtext: I am sure the committee was pleased to hear from the minister today that he and his officials had scrutinized in detail every item of the estimates and on this side of the house particularly we were pleased and not surprised to hear the minister say that no waste or extravagance were found in the department. In connection with this vote, which provides for a payment to McGill University in connection with the development of a coal-fired gas turbine, I am not asking the minister for a scientific course on the experiment made to date but I think the house and the people of the country have a right to know how far the experiment has gone, what stage it has reached, if it is practicable and what results have been obtained to date.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I expected that question. I presume that the hon. member refers to the Mordell project conducted by McGill University at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Quebec. I have some notes here that I have prepared on the subject. The experimental plant at Ste. Anne de Bellevue was subjected to its final program of test running in 1956. Considerable data was accumulated during that period. A conference on coal-burning gas turbines, planned by Professor Mordell, was arranged to coincide with the final operations in November, 1956. Representatives from Canada, the United States, Britain, South Africa and Australia attended the conference where the results of the Mordell project experiment were discussed in the light of world developments in coal-fired gas turbines. The final editing of the proceedings of the conference should be available very shortly.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
The experiment has now reached the stage where the participation of industry or power utilities is necessary for its future development and utilization as an economical power unit. Though there is little hope now of producing a coal-fired gas turbine locomotive that would stem the tide of the rapid dieseliza-tion of our Canadian railways, the coal-fired gas turbine could find an application in the field of small power generating stations, particularly where lack of water prohibits the use of a steam plant. It also seems that the gas turbine combined with a steam plant could improve thermal efficiency and reduce water requirements.
I might give the following by way of a resume. The agreement between the department and McGill University was signed in October, 1950. Its purpose was research to improve the utilization of Canadian coal through the developing of a coal-fired gas turbine operating on a design of Professor Mordell, to be used in locomotives and stationary power plants. In November, 1953, the experimental plant was completed and trial runs, testing and experimenting were conducted during 1954, 1955 and 1956. In 1957 $25,000 was provided to maintain a staff for the completion of reports and to pay for expenses in housing the plant at Ste. Anne de Bellevue. For 1958 no moneys are to be provided in the estimates.

The last time this matter was before the house was in the summer of 1956 when the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys were under consideration. At that time the then minister of mines and technical surveys informed the house that the experiment was proceeding but that difficulties were being experienced with the heat exchanger and the combustion chamber of this particular engine.
He went on to say that it was intended that a symposium would be held in the fall of 1956 to evaluate the experiment. He further told the house that Professor Mordell was very optimistic that this particular experiment would reach the practical stage. I believe that already the parliament of Canada has voted $700,000 or more for this project. We have not been told today at what stage the project is, whether it has any practical application and whether any effort is to be made by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to develop the project to

This question of the coal-fired gas turbine has come up almost every year for the last 10 or 15 years. As was indicated by one of the previous speakers, we who are from the coal mining areas have been very interested in the progress made on this project. I recall on one occasion the then minister of mines and technical surveys made a speech in which he forecast that it would not be very long before our coal mines would come back to life again because of the tremendous amount of coal that would be used in this type of engine. We all had great hopes that this was going to be the solution for our declining coal mines, but so far we have not seen any results.
I see now that this vote has been reduced by $75,000. This means that in effect there will not be much progress made in the future. It was difficult for me to hear what the minister was saying, but from what he said I took it the department has not given up the idea of developing a coal-fired gas turbine for railway locomotives; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I would say the government has not given up hope of developing such a gas turbine but it cannot be produced in time to stop dieselization. It will take some time before a final conclusion can be reached about these experiments. However, a gas turbine cannot be prepared in time to stop dieselization.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I understand that the minister has not given up hope, although he has given up research. I make that remark because the estimate has been cut down by $75,000, and that is certainly going to prevent very much increase in research. I would take it also from what the minister has just said that he has hopes that research will be continued in an endeavour to have this gas turbine used in railway locomotives. This was the purpose of development, but now I understand that development work has ceased and that the department is turning the information they have over to commercial organizations to use in a small way.
If that is the case, then all this stuff we have been told over the last years was just so much lukewarm water, if I may use that expression. Only last year we were told that the government had tremendous hopes for

this project; just be patient, they said, and almost any time now this is going to solve our coal problems. I recall quite well that the former minister of trade and commerce, Mr. Howe, was on one of the committees of the house and he told us the project had been sidetracked entirely. Now the minister tells the committee it has been sidetracked but they hope to get it back on the main track later. What are we going to believe? If this government wants to look for places in which to economize I think I could go in as a greenhorn and show them places where they could save a few million dollars. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

The Royal Canadian Geographical Society
Her Majesty the Queen has been graciously pleased to confer the title of "Royal" on the Canadian Geographical Society. This is a mark of appreciation prefixed to the title of those organizations selected by Her Majesty that are deemed worthy to receive such an honour.

With respect to this item on dominion observatories I would like to say a word because I think it is appropriate at this point to make a few remarks in connection with the subject of time, that is time in a legal sense and not in the sense in which it is used by some of my colleagues.

In recent years we in the provinces have instituted daylight saving time and in peacetime the regulations concerning this time, as I understand it, come under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. It is only under war conditions that the federal government has jurisdiction in that respect. I think we in Canada are a most illogical people; we have daylight saving time established in British Columbia during certain months and during somewhat different months in Alberta and in other provinces no daylight saving at all. Now I think that is a lot of nonsense.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

The dominion coal board estimates have been used in the past by hon. members from the coal mining areas as an occasion to discuss conditions in the industry, to place problems before the committee and to enlist support for the measures that are necessary to sustain this industry.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, I regret that the ninth annual report of the dominion coal board which has been tabled has not yet been made available in printed form. This report usually provides a wealth of information and facts and a distillation of trends in the industry which must be studied if suggestions are to fye made to promote. The ninth annual report has, however, been tabled, and it is a very useful document indeed, and the coal board is to be congratulated on the very successful way in which it has analysed the problems of the industry. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that this industry is causing concern, and has been causing concern, to the people of Nova Scotia, and I think any person who has examined conditions in the industry recently has greater cause for concern than ever.
This concern arises because the industry is a shrinking source of employment. The decline in the number of people employed in the coal mines of Nova Scotia during the past year is alarming. The Minister of Labour made s-ome figures available with regard to this matter and the reduction in employment in the three main coal fields in Nova Scotia through the period September 1956 to September 1957 surprised even me, though I realized there had been a sharp decline. The number on the pay rolls in the coal mines of Nova Scotia in September, 1956 was 10,061; the number on the payroll in September of this year was 9,045, a reduction of
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys 1,016. That is a very serious reduction because it represents a reduction of 10 per cent of the working force in a single year. The reduction in employment in the main coal fields is as follows: 226 in the Cape Breton area coal fields, 367 in the Pictou coal field and 423 in the Springhill area coal fields. As I said, this rate of reduction in the number on the payroll is frightening and if continued would in a single decade wipe out the -mining industry in the province of Nova Scotia.
It is not a matter of coincidence that of the four towns in Canada declared to be areas of labour surplus by the Minister of Labour on October 31 in this house two of these centres are located in the coal producing areas of Nova Scotia. In reply to a question asked by the hon. member for New Westminster the Minister of Labour, as reported at page 598 of Hansard of October 31, said in part as follows:
In the second place, Mr. Speaker, when it becomes evident that work is simply not to be had in a certain locality, that activity has dried up and there is little likelihood of work being found, or where the supply of workers is far in excess of the available jobs and will likely remain so, then the Department of Labour has recommended that such areas be declared labour surplus areas and transportation assistance has been supplied to workers who have promises of jobs in other regions. Windsor, Ontario; Springhill and New Glasgow, Nova Scotia; and St. Stephen, New Brunswick, have been declared such areas.
It can be seen that the declaration of the Minister of Labour is not a matter of coincidence because it reflects the trend already outlined in the reduction of the number employed in the coal areas of Nova Scotia. Furthermore the trend in coal output reflects as well the declining employment opportunities. I understand that from the years 1950 to 1956 there has been a decrease in the coal production in the province of Nova Scotia of more than 700,000 tons. I think the figures placed on the record just recently by the hon. member for Bow River show that in the first six months of 1957 there has been a reduction of about 180,000 tons in the coal production of the province of Alberta over the first six months of 1956.
Paralleling the decrease in employment in the mines of Nova Scotia and the drop in production has been an increasing demand for coal for industrial purposes and an enormous relative increase in the importation of United States coal. The hon. member for Bow River put a table on Hansard that will be found at page 1123 showing the fact that in 1956 Canada imported more than 22 million tons of United States coal for consumption in Ontario and Quebec. The dominion coal

Private Bills
board makes the same point on page 6 of its tabled report, as follows:
The production of Canadian coal mines in 1956-57 amounting to 14.3 million tons, showed a decrease of 819,000 tons from the total for 1955-56. The loss was incurred mostly by the Alberta and British Columbia fields, but was also shared to an appreciable extent by those of Nova Scotia. Imports of bituminous coal for the comparative period were up 2.9 million tons but the importation of anthracite continued to decline.
The dominion coal board clearly underlines the fact that while the production of coal in Canada declined the general demand for coal increased and these demands were met in the period I have mentioned by the importation into Canada of almost three million additional tons of United States bituminous coal. How perplexing and frustrating it is to coal miners in Nova Scotia facing difficulties in their source of livelihood to observe these increasing demands for coal met from United States sources. Nova Scotia sells little if any coal in the province of Ontario and in any event has sold no coal in that area since 1950. We sell an increasing percentage of our output, however, in the province of Quebec, amounting in 1956 to 40.2 per cent of the total sale of Nova Scotia coal. Notwithstanding its supplies from Nova Scotia, however, the province of Quebec satisfies 58 per cent of its requirements from the United States. The fact that we are able at all to supply this market in Quebec is the result of the subvention policy that has been in existence in this country since 1928. The subvention policy has been our indispensable and successful weapon against the further encroachment of United States coal.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to dissolve the Ottawa and New York Railway Company. This company is a wholly owned subsidiary of the New York Central Railroad Company. It was incorporated in 1882 and its act of incorporation was amended from time to time until 1898. The company owns the right of way known as the New York Central Railway line from Cornwall to Ottawa. That railway line was

operated by the New York Central Railroad Company, and in 1952 the operating company discontinued the passenger service on the line.
In January of 1957 the board of transport commissioners for Canada authorized the abandonment of the line and the line has now been removed and there is in existence only the right of way. The right of way has been sold to the Canadian National Railway Company.
In addition to the railway line, the company owned a bridge at or very close to Cornwall known as the Roosevelt bridge. That bridge, as will be recalled by hon. members, carried vehicular traffic as well as railroad traffic. The removal of the bridge became necessary by virtue of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and in accordance with the requirements of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. That meant that the railway line lost its connecting link with the New York Central system in the United States.
All outstanding accounts owing by the company have been paid but so that there will be no possibility of any unknown accounts appearing and no assets available to provide for them, the bill provides that the parent company, the New York Central Railroad Company, is liable for all claims, debts, causes of action and so on of the company. the second reading of Bill No. 31, respecting the Rio de Janeiro Tramway, Light and Power Company, Limited.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I, by way of introduction to the four bills with which I am concerned, make the preliminary statement that these bills concern the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company Limited and three of its subsidiaries, namely, the Rio de Janeiro Tramway, Light and Power Company Limited, the Sao Paulo Electric Company Limited and the Brazilian Hydro

Electric Company Limited. Briefly, the purpose of the first three bills is to transfer the head offices of the subsidiaries from Canada to Brazil. This is brought about by the difficulty of public financing in Brazil without becoming Brazilian companies, and it is the purpose of these bills to transfer the head offices so that these companies may take advantage of Brazilian regulations to become Brazilian companies.
May I state that representatives of the company will be present before the standing committee to answer any questions for which I may not have the answer today. Perhaps I should, as a matter of record, make a few preliminary observations. The Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company is a Canadian company incorporated by letters patent dated July 12, 1912 under the Companies Act of Canada and has its head office in the city of Toronto, Ontario. The company, through its subsidiaries, operates companies engaged in furnishing electric power, telephone, gas and tramway services in the United States of Brazil.
The company's investment in Brazil is in excess of $900 million, this amount being represented by its investment in the shares and obligations of its subsidiary operating companies. The subsidiary operating companies are corporations which were incorporated in various jurisdictions, including Canada, Ontario, England and Belgium. Since the end of world war II Brazil, like our own country, has had a tremendous period of development and the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company is making every effort to keep pace and to facilitate Brazil's development through carrying on an extensive program to meet the various demands for light, transportation, telephones, etc. But it is having difficulty in financing to the extent that it finds, in order to take advantage of obtaining local financing in Brazil, it must become a Brazilian company.
In 1953 two of the subsidiaries of this company transferred their head offices to Brazil. One was a dominion company and the other was a company incorporated under the laws of the province of Ontario. The reason that they would like to use the legal fiction of remaining a person and of maintaining their present capacity as a company and not forming a new company in Brazil is to overcome the cost that might be incurred by reason of the various transfer taxes that would be applied against them in Brazil. It also avoids the tremendous timeconsuming and costly task of evaluating the assets of each subsidiary which would be required under Brazilian law. It also avoids 96698-92
Private Bills
the necessity of transfers and the assumption by a new company of the obligations and liabilities of the present company. It also avoids the necessity of having to transfer the concessions, a difficult and complex problem due to the number of concessions involved which would affect various governments in Brazil. The present method will make the task easier.
As I said before, the first step in the implementation of this policy was in December, 1953 when the Brazilian Telephone Company, one of the principal subsidiary operating companies of Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company Limited, applied to the parliament of Canada for a private act authorizing the transfer of its head office to Brazil. The application of this company was favourably considered by parliament and an act entitled "An act respecting Brazilian Telephone Company", being chapter 74 of the Statutes of Canada, 1953-54, 2-3 Elizabeth II, was then passed. The practical solution of the matter is based on the fact that article 71 of the Brazilian corporation law, decree-law No. 2627 of September 29, 1940, states:
A foreign corporation authorized to carry on business in Brazil may be nationalized, subject to authorization of the federal government, by transferring its head office to Brazil.
It is also based on the legal theory set out in our law and covered by the Bonanza Creek Gold Mining Company case, cited as 1916, No. 1 appeal cases, at 566 and also cited as 85 L.J. P.C. 114, where a company has the capacity to apply for and accept a decree under the Brazilian corporation law, under which it would adopt Brazilian nationality. It is also considered on the basis of Mr. Justice Duff's remarks in the case of The Canadian Bank of Commerce versus Cud-worth Rural Telephone Company, 1923 Supreme Court Reports, page 618, where it was stated that it was necessary to obtain a special act of the parliament of Canada to provide authority to transfer the head office out of Canada.
With this background, therefore, I should like to present first of all Bill No. 31 which concerns the Rio de Janeiro Tramway, Light and Power Company Limited, which company was incorporated in 1904 under the Companies Act of Canada, 1902. The two acts respecting the company were passed by the parliament of Canada, first in 1904 by which the name of the company was changed and its objects expanded to contain authorization to carry on a street railway business, and the second act in 1906 by which the company was authorized to issue bearer share warrants and to guarantee certain kinds of

obligations of companies subsidiary to or controlled by it. The authorized capital of the company is $50 million divided into 50,000 shares of the par value of $100 each.
The company is engaged in the business of generating and distributing electric power in the state of Rio de Janeiro and in the federal district, which includes the city of Rio de Janeiro, and in the operation of a street railway service in the federal district. It is also engaged in the manufacture and distribution of gas for domestic and commercial purposes through a subsidiary company in Rio de Janeiro.

He said: Mr. Speaker, briefly the purpose of this bill is to enable the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited, the parent company of the companies of which we have been talking, to come under the regular provisions of the Companies Act and not to be limited in its number of directors as it presently is.

Section 76 of that act at that time limited the maximum number of directors of the companies under it to 15. In 1914 the company obtained a special act of the parliament of Canada, being chapter 131 of the statutes of 1914 entitled "An Act respecting Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited" which reads in part as follows:
5. Notwithstanding the provisions of section 76 of the Companies Act, the company may, by by-law in the manner provided in the said section, increase the number of its directors to not more than twenty.

Then in 1918 the limitation on the maximum number of directors was removed from the Companies Act and since that time the Companies Act has not contained any limitation on the maximum number of directors. However, the company still remains or continues under the handicap or limitation of this section that was passed in 1914. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext: Here in Ottawa. Now if this court sits in Ottawa it means that a court of divorce would be imposed upon Quebec and Newfoundland which we do not want. We will therefore oppose that measure if another bill comes before the house because we oppose any court of divorce in Quebec, and I think the same applies in Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext: The hon. member has one right now and he is a member of it, this House of Commons.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
