speechtext:
Yes, but it has
been accepted by parliament, I believe, in the previous years that this procedure could be dealt with by parliament. The hon. gentleman now wants to change that procedure and we feel that, in this change, he is trying to impose upon Quebec and Newfoundland a court of divorce which we do not want. For that reason we are opposed to changing the existing procedure and as I say, we are firmly opposed to divorce in my province.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext:
I am
not so much concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the procedure but I have heard nothing in this house in the years during which I have been here to indicate that anybody was concerned about a cure for divorce itself. The cause of divorce is selfishness and the use of strong drink and until we get such a cure- which really is the absolute surrender to the Prince of Peace-we are going to have divorce and we are going to have trouble with it. This is the breaking up of home life and the

Christian home is the bulwark of the nation which is what we have to fight for.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am sure we all agree with the hon. member for Fort William. Nevertheless, that does not dispose of the situation, because if there were just one case of divorce coming from certain provinces in this country there would be no way in which that one divorce could be granted except in accordance with the manner now followed.
I do not know how to handle this thing, either, Mr. Speaker. 1 have given a lot of thought to it over the years. On occasions I have joined my voice with some in the C.C.F. group requesting that consideration be given to some other form of proceeding with these divorces, a form which would avoid bringing them before parliament but, frankly,
I do not know of any other way in which it can be done while preserving the civil rights of the provinces of this country. That is the conclusion I am reaching.
I know it is nauseating, sometimes, for us to get piles and piles of evidence so exhaustive that we can never read it all, and yet have to pass bills on a limited understanding of them. In my experience I have had to deal, in a way, with matters of this kind.
I have been brought in and asked to deal with various types of domestic problems; I have watched while cases were being heard in the courts of the land, and I will say this: I doubt very much whether the criticism which has sometimes been levelled at those who hear the evidence and make recommendations in another place is altogether warranted. I must confess that I, myself, have sometimes levelled mild criticism in that direction, but having a little experience, as I said, in hearing some cases tried in some of the courts of the country, and having heard some cases presented before the committee of the other place, I am going to suggest that the cases heard by the committee of the senate are just as thoroughly heard as they are by any other court.
These committees are regularly constituted and when the committee has to divide itself into sub-committees I am confident that they choose able men to act as chairman of those sub-committees, usually lawyers of some repute, and I am quite certain that they are as able as some I have known who have been appointed judges. The committee does its best possible work. Much as we may dislike the method which we have to follow, and much as we may dislike divorce, the problem still faces us, and it seems to me to be almost insurmountable. It is difficult to see how this could be dealt with in any other way.
(Mr. Mclvor.]
I object just as much as anyone to the necessity for this procedure but at the same time the question has to be dealt with and it appears to me that it will be dealt with in the way it is now for a long time to come.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? In view of what he has said about the satisfactory way in which he says the senate committee deals with these cases, would he be inclined to recommend that they should deal with these cases finally, in which case they would not have to come to us?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend means that that committee should constitute a kind of judicial court or court of record, call it what you like, I would be quite willing that that should happen, because my own view is that the method of being heard by the senate and then the case coming here is something that is unnecessary, although there have been times when the odd, individual case has been reheard by the private bills committee and rejected even though the senate had recommended it.
But perhaps that could be remedied too; perhaps there could be provision for an appeal if one or other of the parties involved did not think he or she had received a fair hearing. But I should be quite willing to have an arrangement of the kind suggested by the hon. member, if that could be done. However, I doubt very much whether it could.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very long in speaking on this matter at this particular time, though, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I reserve my right to say more, possibly at a later date this session.
I fail to appreciate, once again, how we, elected as legislators, can be expected to act as adjudicators of our own legislation. I think that is an absolutely wrong course of action. Some hon. members may feel that they are not participating in a divorce court, but I contend that they are by the very fact that they are members of the House of Commons and have the right to pass a vote on these acts.
I regret that I fail to appreciate the thought which was expressed that we in the C.C.F. group want to force the divorce court upon anybody. I want to see that fair play exists, and that justice is done to these people, and we feel that when a group of legislators suddenly switches, at five o'clock into a group of judges, the fair deal to which these people are entitled cannot possibly be given them.
I regret very much that I have not the same confidence in the judicial capacity of the

members of the other place as a few hon. members have expressed. I have often had the feeling that no member of the other place above even the age of 60 ought to have the right even to sit in on one of these cases.
I am going to close my remarks this afternoon by hoping that the sponsor, who is acting in a responsible position, has at least read all the bills.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext: How old are you?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS-SENATE BILLS
speechtext: I would also express the hope that all members of this house have looked carefully over the list of names because whether they know it or not it is technically possible for their own names to appear here and for this house to grant a divorce without their being aware that they are voting on their own cases.

MEXICO TRAMWAYS COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 73, an act respecting Mexico Tramways Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes which remain before six o'clock I think I can very briefly explain the essence of this bill. There is a considerable printed explanation which I think can be compressed into these facts. This company was incorporated in 1906 and then wished to take on additional
functions including the operation of a tramway in Mexico. At that time a company incorporated under the Companies Act was not permitted to do so without a special act and enabling legislation was enacted by this house. Subsequently this company went out of the tramway business in Mexico. It no longer wishes to pursue this endeavour and it is now asking that chapter 125 be revoked so that it may effect a return to what it wishes to be, an investment company, retaining the name Mexico Tramways Company but coming under the Companies Act under which in due time the name of this company will be changed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Monday will be private members' day and an arrangement has been reached between the parties under which on Tuesday we will move to go into supply and we will discuss exclusively external affairs. If there should be a vote it is agreed that it will take place at ten o'clock rather than at 8.15 as provided under the rules.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, do I understand we are limiting the debate on external affairs to one day?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, it has been agreed that one day would be allotted for that purpose. Mind you, the estimates will then be referred to the standing committee on external affairs as has been customary for some years.

speechtext:
Is

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am not in a position to say for sure but I believe arrangements have been made or are in process of being made for Wednesday to put through in all stages the bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act and probably we would then go on with estimates. Thursday is to be a private members' day and on Friday we would take either estimates or legislation. I am not certain at the moment which it will be.
